title: Tiu v. Platinum Plans Philippines
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the validity of a non-compete clause in an employment contract, provided it is reasonable in terms of duration, geographical scope, and the nature of the restriction. The clause must be necessary to protect the employer's legitimate business interest.
doctrine: Non-compete clauses in employment contracts are valid and enforceable provided they are: (1) reasonable as to duration and geographical scope; (2) necessary to protect the employer's legitimate business interests; and (3) not unduly oppressive on the employee's right to earn a livelihood. The restraint must be limited to what is reasonably necessary.
fullText:
NACHURA, J.:

The issue is the validity and enforceability of a non-compete clause in the employment contract between the petitioner and the respondent company.

The freedom to contract is both a constitutional and statutory right. Article 1306 of the Civil Code provides that the contracting parties may establish such stipulations, clauses, terms, and conditions as they may deem convenient, provided they are not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order, or public policy.

A non-compete clause, while constituting a restraint on the employee's right to pursue a livelihood, is valid if it is reasonable and necessary to protect the employer's legitimate business interests.
